ta-l1d3q2-d1e97.summary: Transitional paragraph opening the inquiry into the vestige (vestigium) of the Trinity in creatures, in three articles: what a vestige is, what its parts are, and whether it is found in every creature.

ta-l1d3q2-d1e109.summary: First objection that the Creator's likeness in creatures cannot be called a vestige. A vestige is that by which a thing is traced (investigatur), but God's majesty is untraceable: his ways are unsearchable (Rom. 11:33), and his footprints will not be known (Ps. 76:20).
claims: God's ways are unsearchable, so his likeness cannot serve as a trace.

ta-l1d3q2-d1e118.summary: Second objection. A vestige is an impression following the motion of the one who leaves it, but God produces things without any motion of his own (James 1:17).
claims: A vestige follows the motion of its maker, and God acts without motion.

ta-l1d3q2-d1e124.summary: Third objection. A vestige in the present sense leads to knowledge of the persons, but creatures cannot give knowledge of the Trinity (as established). So creaturely likeness is not a vestige, or the vestige does not lead to the Trinity.
claims: Creatures cannot yield knowledge of the Trinity.

ta-l1d3q2-d1e128.summary: Fourth objection. Gregory, on Job 11:7, says God's vestiges are the kindness of his visitation by which he shows us the way. So a vestige is not the divine likeness in creatures.
claims: Gregory identifies God's vestiges with the benevolence of his visitation.

ta-l1d3q2-d1e134.summary: Thomas's determination. 'Vestige' is used metaphorically, after the literal footprint, an impression that leads confusedly to knowledge of something because it represents it only in part (the foot) and only in its lower surface. Three things belong to the concept of a vestige: likeness, imperfection of the likeness, and that it leads to the thing whose vestige it is. Creatures bear an imperfect likeness of the Creator through which we can come to know him, so they are called his vestige. Because they fall further short of representing the distinction of persons than the essential attributes, the creature is more properly called a vestige insofar as it leads to the persons than insofar as it leads to the divine essence.
claims: A vestige involves likeness, imperfection of likeness, and leading to its source.
Creatures are vestiges of God because they bear an imperfect likeness that leads to him.
The creature is a vestige more properly with respect to the persons than to the essence.

ta-l1d3q2-d1e137.summary: Reply to the first objection. God's ways are called unsearchable because we cannot fully comprehend his works, not because we cannot reach them from creatures at all.
claims: God's ways are unsearchable in the sense of not fully comprehensible.

ta-l1d3q2-d1e140.summary: Reply to the second objection. In metaphorical predication it is enough that there be likeness in some respect, not in all; otherwise there would be identity, not likeness.
claims: Metaphor requires likeness in some respect, not in all.

ta-l1d3q2-d1e143.summary: Reply to the third objection. Through the vestige we reach the persons only very confusedly, through what is appropriated to them rather than through what is proper to them. Appropriated features are essential, though they resemble the persons' proper features.
claims: The vestige leads to the persons only confusedly, via appropriated essential attributes.

ta-l1d3q2-d1e146.summary: Reply to the fourth objection. Many things can resemble one thing, so the same word can be transferred to different things by different likenesses. The likeness in creatures can be called a vestige as representing confusedly, and the works of divine goodness shown in the mystery of the incarnation can be called God's vestiges as preparing our way to him.
claims: The same metaphor may apply in different respects, to creaturely likeness and to the works of the incarnation.

ta-l1d3q2-d1e158.summary: First objection, that the vestige should have only two parts. A vestige is a property of the creature, and a creature has only two essential parts, matter and form.
claims: A creature has only two essential parts, matter and form.

ta-l1d3q2-d1e161.summary: Second objection, that there should be four parts. The vestige represents not only the Trinity of persons but also the unity of essence, so it needs three parts for the persons and a fourth for the essence.
claims: The vestige represents the unity of essence as well as the Trinity.

ta-l1d3q2-d1e164.summary: Third objection. The vestige represents the Creator, and creatures participate many divine attributes (Dionysius), so there should be very many parts.
claims: Creatures participate many divine attributes.

ta-l1d3q2-d1e168.summary: Fourth point, raising the question why different authorities assign the parts of the vestige differently: number, weight, and measure (Wis. 11:21), Augustine's mode, species, and order, and others.
claims: Authorities assign the parts of the vestige in different ways.

ta-l1d3q2-d1e177.summary: Thomas's determination. A vestige exists in the creature insofar as it imitates divine perfection. A creature's perfection is not found in its principles, which are imperfect (neither matter nor form has perfect being of itself), but in its being joined to its end. Since nature does not join distant things without a middle, every creature has a beginning, a middle, and an end, the triad by which Pythagoras measured perfection. This triad represents the distinction of persons, the Son being the middle person and the Spirit the terminus of the processions. Because there can be many middles between two extremes, the triad can be assigned in different ways, which explains the different lists. (a) The principles, their inclination toward the being of what they constitute, and their termination under that being give number, weight, and measure. (b) The principles, the form, and the relation to other things give Augustine's 'that it stands, is distinguished, and fits', and correspondingly mode, species, and order, or one, true, and good. (c) The whole thing as perfected by form, its power, and its operation give Dionysius's essence, power, and operation. All these lists share the one common concept of beginning, middle, and end.
claims: The vestige lies in the creature's ordered perfection as beginning, middle, and end.
The triad of beginning, middle, and end represents the distinction of the divine persons.
The various triads (number–weight–measure, mode–species–order, one–true–good, essence–power–operation) are different ways of assigning beginning, middle, and end.

ta-l1d3q2-d1e183.summary: Reply to the first objection. Although the creature has two essential parts, there is also the relation of one to the other and many consequent perfections, by which the parts of the vestige can be assigned.
claims: The parts of the vestige include the relation between matter and form and the perfections that follow.

ta-l1d3q2-d1e186.summary: Reply to the second objection. As in God the essence does not add to the number of the persons, so in the creature its being, which represents the essence, underlies the three parts of the vestige without being counted with them.
claims: The creature's being represents the divine essence and is not counted among the three parts of the vestige.

ta-l1d3q2-d1e189.summary: Reply to the third objection. The creaturely properties that lead us to the divine attributes, though many, are ordered as beginning, middle, and end, under which concepts they lead to the three persons however they are diversified.
claims: Many creaturely properties are ordered under beginning, middle, and end and so lead to the three persons.

ta-l1d3q2-d1e201.summary: First objection, that the vestige is not in every creature. The likeness of a vestige is contrasted with the likeness of an image, and some creatures, like humans, bear the image.
claims: Vestige and image are opposed kinds of likeness.

ta-l1d3q2-d1e204.summary: Second objection. A vestige represents imperfectly, but some creatures, like sanctifying grace by which God dwells in humans, are a perfect likeness of divine goodness.
claims: Sanctifying grace is a perfect likeness of divine goodness.

ta-l1d3q2-d1e207.summary: Third objection. Each part of the vestige, such as mode or species, is itself a creature. If every creature has a vestige, mode would have its own mode, species, and order, and so on to infinity.
claims: If every creature had a vestige, the parts of the vestige would require further parts ad infinitum.

ta-l1d3q2-d1e211.summary: Fourth objection from Ambrose, who says it is the nature of light not to be in number, weight, and measure like other creatures. Light is a creature, so not every creature has the vestige.
claims: Ambrose says light is not in number, weight, and measure.

ta-l1d3q2-d1e217.summary: Fifth objection from Bernard: the mode of charity is to have no mode. Charity, though a creature, lacks mode, species, and order.
claims: Charity is said to have no mode.

ta-l1d3q2-d1e223.summary: Sed contra. Wisdom 11:21 says God disposed all things in number, weight, and measure. Augustine says that where mode, species, and order are great there is great good, where small little good, where absent no good. Every creature is some good, so every creature has these three.
claims: Every creature, being good, has mode, species, and order.

ta-l1d3q2-d1e232.summary: Thomas's determination. The vestige follows on the perfect being a creature receives from God, so it is found simply only in what is perfect in itself, namely individuals in the genus of substance. Accidents, whose being depends on substance, have the vestige only in ordering to substance: they are modes, species, and orders of substances rather than having these themselves (unless God is called their mode, species, and order effectively). Yet since every accident adds some being to the substance, a vestige can be considered with respect to that being. What deprives a thing of an accident deprives it of mode, species, and order with respect to that being. Sin, which deprives of grace, is a privation of mode, species, and order in gracious being while these remain in natural being.
claims: The vestige is found simply in individual substances; in accidents only in ordering to substance.
Sin deprives of mode, species, and order with respect to gracious being but not natural being.

ta-l1d3q2-d1e235.summary: Reply to the first objection. The higher always includes the power of the lower, as the soul includes the power of nature: it is the nature of the body, gives it natural being, and has its own operations besides. The image follows the soul as intellectual, but this does not exclude the vestige, which follows it as a created nature.
claims: The higher includes the power of the lower, so the image in the soul does not exclude the vestige.

ta-l1d3q2-d1e238.summary: Reply to the second objection. Sanctifying grace is called a perfect likeness with respect to what it adds over other creatures, not simply but relative to other created likenesses. In what it shares with other creatures it has the character of a vestige.
claims: Grace is a perfect likeness only relatively, and has the character of a vestige in what it shares with creatures.

ta-l1d3q2-d1e242.summary: Reply to the third objection. Something is 'modified' in two ways: formally, by a mode within it, or effectively, by what imposes mode on it, and in this sense God is the mode of all things. The mode of a creature has no further formal mode, only an effective one, and the same holds for the other parts. This halts the regress.
claims: A creature's mode is not formally modified by a further mode but effectively by God.
God is effectively the mode of all things.

ta-l1d3q2-d1e245.summary: Reply to the fourth objection. Light in itself is created in number, weight, and measure, having finite being and power like other creatures. But relative to other bodily creatures it has an indeterminate power, since all bodies are in some way informed by light and the lower bodies are perfected in their natures through it, as the universal form of the first alterant, the heaven. In this respect it is said not to be created in number, weight, and measure.
claims: Light is finite in itself but indeterminate in power relative to other bodies, as the universal form of the heavens' alteration.

ta-l1d3q2-d1e248.summary: Reply to the last objection. Charity can be considered in two ways. In its being in the subject, it has a mode according to the measure of the recipient's capacity, whether by nature or effort. In its inclination to its object it has no mode, since its infinite object is not proportioned to our will: one can never love God so much that he does not deserve and will to be loved more.
claims: Charity has a mode as received in a subject but none in its inclination to its infinite object.

ta-l1d3q2-d1e260.summary: An expositio textus glossing Lombard's phrases on knowing God from creatures. 'Invisible things', 'power', and 'divinity' are read either as the attributes perfecting God in himself, his productive power, and his role as end, or as works, power, and essence. On the human's 'excellence' over creatures, despite angels' superiority (Ps. 8:6): humans and angels are equal in their ordering to the end, humans are greater in divine restoration because human nature was assumed in the incarnation, and angels are nobler by nature; alternatively, 'world' here means only visible things. The eternity of the Creator is inferred from the perpetuity of creatures because the cause is nobler than the effect. The Son is understood as 'most perfect beauty' because beauty consists in splendour and proportion, and truth has the character of splendour while equality takes the place of proportion.
claims: Humans and angels are equal in their end, humans are greater by the incarnation, and angels are greater by nature.
A cause is nobler than its effect, so perpetual effects imply an eternal cause.
Beauty consists in splendour and proportion, appropriated to the Son as truth and equality.

ta-l1d3q2-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium of Question 2 introduces the treatment of the vestige of the Trinity in creatures in three articles: its nature, its parts, and its universality.

ta-l1d3q2-Dd1e101.summary: Article 1 asks what a vestige is and whether the Creator's likeness in creatures can be called one. Objections cite God's unsearchable ways, God's acting without motion, the impossibility of knowing the Trinity from creatures, and Gregory's identification of vestiges with God's kind visitation. Thomas explains 'vestige' as a metaphor from a footprint, involving likeness, imperfection, and leading to the source. Creatures are vestiges of God, more properly as leading confusedly to the persons than to the essence. The replies note that metaphor needs likeness only in some respect and that the vestige reaches the persons only through appropriated attributes. The incarnation's works can also be called vestiges in another sense.
claims: Creatures are vestiges of God as imperfect likenesses that lead to him.
The vestige leads only confusedly to the persons, through appropriated attributes.

ta-l1d3q2-Dd1e150.summary: Article 2 asks about the parts of the vestige. Objections propose two parts (matter and form), four (adding essence), or many (all participated attributes), and ask why authorities' lists differ. Thomas locates the vestige in the creature's perfection as an ordered triad of beginning, middle, and end, which mirrors the persons, with the Son as middle and the Spirit as terminus. Because many middles can lie between the extremes, the triad is assigned variously as number–weight–measure, mode–species–order, one–true–good, or essence–power–operation, all under one common concept. The creature's being represents the essence without being counted among the three parts.
claims: The parts of the vestige are beginning, middle, and end in the creature's perfection, mirroring the three persons.
The various triads in the authorities are different assignments of the same scheme.

ta-l1d3q2-Dd1e193.summary: Article 3 asks whether the vestige is in every creature. Objections cite the image in humans, the perfect likeness of grace, a regress of modes, Ambrose on light, and Bernard on charity's modelessness. The sed contra cites Wisdom 11:21 and Augustine on mode, species, and order as constitutive of every good. Thomas holds that the vestige is found simply in individual substances and in accidents only in ordering to substance, and that sin deprives of mode, species, and order in gracious but not natural being. The replies explain that the higher includes the lower, so image includes vestige, and that grace is a perfect likeness only relatively. The regress is stopped by God as effective mode. Light is finite in itself but universal in power, and charity has a mode in its subject but none toward its infinite object.
claims: Every creature has the vestige: substances simply, accidents in ordering to substance.
God is the effective, not formal, mode of creatures' modes.
Charity has mode in its subject but none toward its infinite object.

ta-l1d3q2-Dd1e253.summary: The Expositio textus for this part of Distinction 3 glosses Lombard's reading of Romans 1:20 and his creaturely arguments. It covers the human's excellence relative to angels, the inference from perpetual creatures to an eternal Creator, and the appropriation of beauty to the Son as splendour (truth) and proportion (equality).
claims: Beauty consists in splendour and proportion, appropriated to the Son.
Humans and angels are equal in end, humans greater by the incarnation, angels greater by nature.

ta-l1d3q2.summary: Quaestio 2 of Book I, Distinction 3 develops the theory of the vestige of the Trinity in creatures. Article 1 defines the vestige metaphorically as an imperfect likeness that leads to its source, proper especially in relation to the persons, though reached only confusedly through appropriated attributes. Article 2 identifies its parts as the creature's ordered perfection of beginning, middle, and end, mirroring the Father, Son, and Spirit. The various traditional triads (number–weight–measure, mode–species–order, one–true–good, essence–power–operation) are different assignments of that scheme. Article 3 extends the vestige to every creature, simply in substances and derivatively in accidents. It treats sin as a privation of mode, species, and order in gracious being, and resolves difficulties about the image, grace, light, and charity. The Expositio glosses Lombard's text on knowing God through creatures.
claims: Every creature is a vestige of the Trinity through its ordered perfection as beginning, middle, and end.
The traditional triads of Scripture and the Fathers are variant assignments of one scheme.
The vestige is found simply in substances and derivatively in accidents.
